reviewed.packages/web/adwaita-web: Adwaita Sans: A PROGRESSIVE ENHANCEMENT over a system-installed face, not an omission. The typeface does ship — `@gjsify/adwaita-fonts` vendors both Sans TTFs — but the only form that survives a `--app browser` build is a `data:` URI (the target emits one file and no assets, so a relative `url()` 404s), and inlining the two faces costs 2.39 MB / 1.18 MB gzip against this package's 190 KB / 26 KB stylesheet. `--app browser` also has no code splitting (`output.inlineDynamicImports`), so a lazy face would cost the same bytes as an eager one: the choice really is all-or-nothing. So the root entry names the family and the app decides, with `applyAdwaitaFonts()` from `@gjsify/adwaita-web/fonts` — one VALUE import, which is the shape that cannot be silently discarded. What made this an accident rather than a decision until now was `import '@gjsify/adwaita-fonts';` in `src/index.ts`: under css-as-string that resolves to `export default "<css>"`, tree-shakes to a MEASURED 0-byte bundle and exits 0. Revisit when the fonts package ships subsetted woff2 (status/open-todos/fonts.md) — at fontsource-like sizes the default flips. THE TAIL BELOW THE HEADING FAMILY IS PART OF THIS DECISION (#1817), not a separate claim, and the rule keys on the FIRST family only — so it reads as one entry. 'Cantarell' is GNOME's own earlier UI face; 'Inter' is the cross-platform name an app usually has beside it; 'Segoe UI' is the explicit Windows face and stays the portable spelling there, because `system-ui` only reached Segoe UI from Windows 8 and Segoe UI Variable from Windows 11; then `system-ui, -apple-system` so macOS renders the platform UI face rather than Helvetica; and only then the `sans-serif` GENERIC, which asks the host for its DEFAULT — the substitution this whole entry is about. Measured on a Mac carrying neither Adwaita Sans nor Cantarell: the stack as it stood resolved to Helvetica, the one typeface no libadwaita application is meant to look like.
reviewed.packages/web/adwaita-web: Adwaita Mono: Nothing in this workspace ships a mono face at all: `@gjsify/adwaita-fonts` vendors two Sans TTFs, and the upstream `refs/adwaita-fonts/mono/` faces are 1.4-1.5 MB EACH, so committing them is a licensing and size decision that belongs to a human, not to a fix. `--monospace-font-family` therefore heads with 'Adwaita Mono' for the GNOME desktops that have `adwaita-mono-fonts` installed, and falls through `ui-monospace, 'SF Mono', 'Menlo', monospace` everywhere else — which is what the generic tail is for. The reason this entry exists is that the SCSS used to assert the opposite in prose ('Adwaita Mono heads it because @gjsify/adwaita-fonts ships it') while the NativeScript theme carrying the same stack already said the truth. The token's consumers are `.monospace` (_labels.scss), `_action_row.scss`, the data-grid mono cell and `<adw-source-view>` — the last of which read a SECOND, longer stack from a TS literal (`source-view/theme.ts`) until it was pointed at this token, so an editor and a `.monospace` label on one page rendered in different typefaces, and the literal was outside this rule, which reads `.css`/`.scss` only. THE TAIL is the same progression the sans stack is, and had the gap in the other direction (#1817): `ui-monospace` covers macOS and GNOME but reaches Cascadia Mono only from Windows 10 1903, and no Windows face was named at all, so a Windows 10 host without it landed on the `monospace` GENERIC — Times New Roman, whose figures do not line up, which is the one property this stack exists to provide. 'Cascadia Code' (ships with Windows Terminal) and 'Consolas' (every Windows since Vista) are now named before it.
reviewed.packages/nativescript-bridge/adwaita: Ad: Same absent face as adwaita-web's entry, reached from `.adw-data-grid-cell.mono` in `src/theme/adwaita.css`. It is the more honest of the two copies: its comment already said `@gjsify/adwaita-fonts` ships no mono TTF. NativeScript does not load `@font-face` at all — a TTF has to be copied into `App_Resources` and matched by file name (Android) or PostScript name (iOS), which `src/fonts.ts` documents — so even a vendored mono face would not make this stack resolve without an app-side install step.
